title: CJILS Copyediting and Layout Manual
text:
Introduction
Welcome to the official guide for supporting the copyediting process of manuscripts submitted to the Canadian Journal of Information and Library Science (CJILS). This resource is designed to assist the journal editors, managers, and copyeditors editors in preparing CJILS articles for publication—ensuring clarity, consistency, and compliance with journal style.
Whether you’re a seasoned language professional or newly joining the CJILS editorial workflow, this guide provides step-by-step instructions, templates, checklists, and formatting support tailored to the specific needs of our journal.

title: Overview
text:
Introduction
This documentation is for CJILS Production Managers, Copyeditors, and Layout Editors and gives a detailed description of the roles and responsibilities for each. All production processes are managed through the CJILS OJS instance hosted by the University of Western Ontario. link Currently, we are using OJS 3.3 for this journal. You can reference PKP documentation here or a video playlist here. OJS will be updated to 3.5 in mid-October to mid-December of 2026.
Additionally, we use an subscription to Overleaf for formatting the proofs and final versions of each work. You can find the login for our Overleaf account here. More details on how to set up each Overleaf project will be included in the Copyediting section below.
Our Google Drive for supporting documents referenced below can be found here.
Overall, our workflow starts with the manuscript submission from an author or authors. If selected by the Chief Editor, it will be assigned to the Production Manager to send out requests for peer-review. Upon receiving peer-reviews, the Production Manager sends the reviews or recommendations to the authors. If revisions are required, the authors may resubmit another version for consideration by the Chief Editor who will determine if another round of reviews is necessary. If approved to move forward, the work then enters the Copyediting stage where the Production Manager will assign a CopyEditor. Once the Copyeditor has created a copy for revisions, it is sent to the author for review and comment. If approved, it moves forward to the Layout Editor and a proof is sent to the authors for their approval. Upon approval, the Final Proof is created and then sent to the authors for a final check. Once approved, the work is then scheduled for publication. Below, we have detailed steps for each process.

title: Overview
text:
Copyediting

Copyeditor Role
The copyeditor:

removes redundancies and repetition,
ensures compliance with the journal’s bibliographic style,
corrects typographic errors, and problems with spelling, punctuation and grammar.

The copyeditor does not change or challenge the substance of the work. If there are concerns about the substance, they should be discussed with the editor before the article is sent back to the author. Authors and copyeditors share responsibility for correct citations. While the burden is proportionally on the author, copyeditors should also double check for accuracy, to the best of their ability. Copyeditors may not have access to all sources; if in doubt, flag an item for the author to recheck. Copyeditors liaise directly with the authors about changes to the manuscript. However, if you have any comments or questions that you are unsure of sending to the author, you may contact the Editor for feedback.

Workload:
Our goal is to spread the workload as evenly as possible so you may receive submissions at any point during the year.


Basic Production Process:

The Copyeditor downloads the Draft file and makes copyedits using Track Changes.
The Copyeditor sends the article with revisions back to the author.
The author makes changes and returns the article back to the Copyeditor.
The Copyeditor prepares a clean, edited copy and notifies the Production Editor that it is ready for layout.
The Layout Editor will apply CJILS formatting and prepare a galley.
The proof will be sent to the author for review and returns the article back to the editors.
That proof will be sent to the Proofreader to scan for any copyediting or formatting errors and returns the article back to the editors.
The Layout Editor then makes any changes, prepares metadata, and prepares accessibility features.
The article is ready for publication.



Production Timeline:
The table below shows the production timeline for each article. For most submissions, the initial copyedit, final copyedit and final proofread should be completed and returned within two weeks. The timeline below also applies to the authors’ copyedits and proofreading (unless there are particularly substantial changes; defer to the Editor if you have any questions).











Copyedit 1
(2 weeks)
Author CE
(2 week)
Copyedit 2
(2 week)
Layout
(2 weeks)
Author Proof
(1 week)
Final Proof
(2 weeks)|



If you believe you will be unable to complete a submission in the usual time frame, please contact the Production Editor to let them know. Depending on your availability, the timeline may either be adjusted or reassigned to another copyeditor.


Copyeditor Tasks and Workflow in OJS
The copyediting stage is intended to improve the readability of the writing: flow, clarity, grammar, wording, and formatting. It also represents the last chance for the author to make substantial changes to the text, as the next stage is restricted to typos and formatting corrections. Refer to the Copyeditor Tasks and Workflow in OJS for instructions on downloading/uploading files and communicating with authors and editors during the copyediting process.

You are now ready to request that the author complete the Author Copyedit.

Copyediting and Style Guide
Copyeditors and Proofreaders use the provided CJILS Copyediting and Style Guide document for instructions on how to edit and style the articles. We ask that you follow this closely and complete the copyediting checklist.


Copyediting with Microsoft Word’s Track Changes
Track Changes (under Tools in the menu bar) enables the copyeditor to make insertions (text appears in color) and deletions (text appears crossed out in color or in the margins as deleted). You can insert comments to ask for clarification or make suggestions. The author should leave those changes with which they are satisfied. If further changes are necessary, the author can make changes to the initial insertions or deletions, as well as make new insertions or deletions elsewhere in the text. After the text has been reviewed by the author, the copyeditor will make a final pass over the text accepting the changes in preparation for the layout and galley stage. The copyeditor’s final copy should be a clean copy, free of any comments or track changes.

title: Overview
text:
Proofreading
The proofreading stage is intended to catch any errors in spelling, grammar, punctuation, and formatting. More substantial changes cannot be made at this stage, unless discussed with the Editor.

Tasks and Workflow in OJS
The Proofreader will be sent the proof via the Production Discussions panel by the Production Editor. To download the article, open the discussion and download the attachment. To send back with any changes, use “Add Message” in the discussion to attach the file and send back to the editors.

Copyediting/Style Guide and Layout
Proofreaders also use the provided CJILS Copyediting and Style Guide document for instructions on how to edit and style the articles. Proofreaders also use the Layout documents to proofread the formatting and layout of the articles.


For Spelling, Grammar, and Style Errors
Use the comments tool in Adobe to request corrections. Provide “CHANGE-TO” instructions to the editor as follows. Highlight the text in question and provide instructions such as:

CHANGE… then the others TO… than the others
CHANGE… Malinowsky TO… Malinowski



For Formatting Errors
Use the comments tool in Adobe to request corrections. Provide “FORMATTING” instructions to the editor as follows:

FORMATTING The numbers in Table 3 are not aligned in the third column.
FORMATTING The paragraph that begins “This last topic…” is not indented.

title: Checklist
Checklist
text:
Editing Checklists

CJILS Specific Requirements

Does the first page include all the required information (title, author names, institution, abstract, keywords, Orcid ID if known)?
Are the authors’ names and institution correct?
Is an abstract of the correct kind included (50-100 words in length)?
Is it unblinded? If not, check in with the Production Editor.
Is the About the Author(s) statement properly positioned and marked?
Are acknowledgements, if added, properly positioned and marked?
Do the references have DOIs or links where applicable? Do the links work?
Does the manuscript follow Chicago Author-Date style? Including in-text citations and references?



Level 1. Checklist for mechanical style and format of text

Is the manuscript complete?
Are all files with tables etc. included?
If an appendix is included, is it properly positioned and marked?
Are endnotes/footnotes, if any, clearly positioned and linked to their indicator symbols in the text?
Are spelling and punctuation consistent? Is the spacing after punctuation correct?
Are extracts and quotations clearly indicated and acknowledged?
Are capital letters, small capitals, italics, and bold type clearly marked and used correctly and consistently?
Are abbreviations and symbols used correctly and consistently? Are abbreviations other than recognized abbreviations for units explained at first mention and later used consistently?
Are special scripts and accents clearly presented and used consistently?
Are numerals correctly written? (see below)
Are parentheses and brackets properly paired off?



Level 2. Checklist for tables and figures

Are tables and figures referred to in the text in correct numerical order?
Do tables and figures show what the text says they show?
Do numbers and other references to table and figure contents match any details cited in the text?


Tables

Do tables have clear titles, column headings, and footnotes, as needed?
Have abbreviations in tables been explained?
Is the arithmetic in tables correct — do numbers in table columns add up correctly, and are percentages correct?



Figures

Are line drawings clearly drawn?
Are photographs of good quality?
If figures have been supplied electronically, are size and resolution acceptable?




Level 3. Checklist for citations and bibliographical references

Are all citations in the text included in the reference list?
Are all references in the list cited in the text?
Are in-text citations and references unblinded?
If names and dates are given in the text, do they agree with those in the list?
Does the form of citations in the text match Chicago Author-Date?
Are all the required parts of references included in the reference list according to Chicago Author-Date?
Are those parts in the correct sequence and form?
Is the punctuation correct?
Is the typographical style (case, italics, bold) correct?
If journal titles are abbreviated, are abbreviations correct?
Does the form of references to books, reports, and other types of publication match the Chicago Author-Date?
Are DOIs and links to e-articles present and valid?



Level 4. A checklist for language editing

Spelling and punctuation

Is the spelling correct and consistent, according to house style?
Are quotation marks correctly used according to Chicago Author-Date?
Are parentheses correctly placed?
Are commas correctly used?
Are hyphens and en and em dashes correctly used with proper spacing?
Have apostrophes been kept to a minimum and been correctly used?
Are colons and semicolons correctly used?
Have exclamation marks and dashes been kept to a minimum?



Grammar and syntax

Has the passive voice been kept to a reasonable minimum?
Are tenses used correctly and consistently?
Have strings of three or more nouns been kept to a minimum?
Have words been used in the right order?



Usage

Is usage correct according to current recommendations?
Have words been used with precision?
Have the simplest words and the simplest ways of writing been used?
Have sexist, racist, or dehumanizing terms been transformed or removed?

Adapted from O’Connor, Maeve, Margaret Cooter, and Sylwia B. Ufnalska. “1.1: Copy-editing scientific papers.” P. Smart, H. Maisonneuve & A. Polderman, eds (2013).

title: Style Guide
text:
Spelling
Use the Chicago Style Guide as your guide.
House style for spelling is Canadian, except when directly citing a source which uses different spelling. Spelling, including hyphenation, should be consistent throughout the manuscript—except for quotations, which must retain the spelling of the original, whether correct or incorrect.

title: Style Guide
text:
Special cases:

ereaders and ebooks (not eBooks)
internet (not Internet)
right-click and right-clicking (not right click)

html or other code as depicted in articles should be done with <> tags, (E.g., “We use the  tag to indicate …”)

Otherwise, standard Canadian spelling includes:

Kilometer and kilometre are both acceptable

title: Style Guide
text:
Punctuation

Commas
Pay careful attention to the Chicago guidelines for using commas. They are usually overused by authors. Use the Oxford Comma, in citations and in regular text. E.g. Associated events can include author interviews, pubcrawls, lectures, online discussions, or even canoe trips.


Em Dashes
Use em dashes sparingly to provide more emphasis than commas and parentheses can provide. Refer to the Chicago Style Guide when doing so. Do not use a space before or after the dashes.

Example:
Organizers must identify cultural literacies—unique to every MRE—that may act as barriers to participation.

To generate an em dash (roughly equivalent to the width of an uppercase M, in contrast to the ndash, which is as wide as an N) hold down Alt and press 0, 1, 5, 1 on your numeric keypad (or holding down Fn and Alt, on newer keyboards without a separate numpad). Or just copy it from here: —


Quotations
Punctuation sits inside quotation marks, even if the punctuation isn’t actually part of the quote.


Colons and Semicolons
Use a colon to join two independent clauses when you wish to emphasize the second clause.

Example:
Road construction in Dallas has hindered travel around town: parts of Main, Fifth, and West Street are closed during the construction.

Use a colon after an independent clause when it is followed by a list, a quotation, appositive, or other ideas directly related to the independent clause.

Example:
Julie went to the store for some groceries: milk, bread, coffee, and cheese.

If the clause following the colon is itself a complete sentence, it should begin with a capital letter.

Examples:
Freud (1930) wrote of two urges: an urge toward union with others and an egoistic urge toward happiness.
They have agreed on the outcome: Informed participants perform better than do uninformed participants.

Use a semicolon to join two independent clauses when the second clause restates the first or when the two clauses are of equal emphasis.

Example:
Road construction in Dallas has hindered travel around town; streets have become covered with bulldozers, trucks, and cones.

Use a semicolon to join two independent clauses when the second clause begins with a conjunctive adverb (however, therefore, moreover, furthermore, thus, meanwhile, nonetheless, otherwise) or a transition (in fact, for example, that is, for instance, in addition, in other words, on the other hand, even so).

Example:
Terrorism in the United States has become a recent concern; in fact, the concern for America’s safety has led to an awareness of global terrorism.

Use a semicolon to join elements of a series when individual items of the series already include commas.

Example:
Recent sites of the Olympic Games include Athens, Greece; Salt Lake City, Utah; Sydney, Australia; Nagano, Japan.



Bullet Points
Bullet points should start with a capital and end with a period. Alternatively, if you wish to create a sentence structure with your list, you can end each item on the list with a semicolon (and the final item with a period).


Hyphenation
See section 7.81-89 of the Chicago Style Guide online for the hyphenation guide. In general, Chicago prefers a spare hyphenation style: if no suitable example or analogy can be found either in this section (7.81–89) or in the dictionary, hyphens should be added only if doing so will prevent a misreading or otherwise significantly aid comprehension. But, the reverse is also true: If the compound adjective is clear as it stands, you do not need a hyphen. This may sound like a judgment call, but the following guidelines can help you make the call in many cases. Adverbs ending in -ly are understood to modify the word that follows. Adding a hyphen would be redundant. For example, in the phrase “widely attended gatherings” readers understand that widely modifies attended. Adding a hyphen, to write this as “widely-attended gatherings,” would not give the reader any additional information.
More info available here: https://www-chicagomanualofstyle-org.proxy1.lib.uwo.ca/book/ed17/part2/ch07/psec089.html
Example relevant cases:

“Information-seeking behaviour” not “information seeking behaviour”
“On” or “off campus” as a place and “off-campus” as a descriptor (off-campus access, off-campus students)
“Full-text downloads” (instead of full text downloads)

title: Style Guide
text:
Grammar

Plural Nouns
“Data” is a plural noun so must be followed by a verb in the plural.

Example:
Once approval was granted from the University Ethics Review Board, the survey data were collected using the online survey tool.



Tense
Select tense carefully. By using verb tenses consistently, you can help ensure smooth expression. Past tense (e.g., “Smith showed,”) or present perfect tense (e.g., “researchers have shown”) or present tense (e.g. Smith presents similar results) are all appropriate for the literature review. Stay within the chosen tense. Use past tense (e.g., “Anxiety decreased significantly”) to describe the results. Use the present tense (e.g., “the results of Experiment 2 indicate”) to discuss implications of the results and to present the conclusions. By reporting the conclusions in the present tense, you allow readers to join you in deliberating the matter at hand.


That/Which
That clauses are essential to the meaning of the sentence (the materials that worked well in the first experiment were used in the second experiment). Which clauses can merely add further information (non-restrictive) or can be essential to the meaning (restrictive) of the sentence.

Restrictive: The cards that worked well in the first experiment were not useful in the second experiment.
Non-restrictive: The cards, which worked well in the first experiment, were not useful in the second experiment.

Consistent use of that for restrictive clauses and which for non-restrictive clauses, which are set off with commas, will help you make your writing clear and precise.

title: Style Guide
text:
Citations
Refer to the Chicago Style Guide for citation specifics or use the Author-Date Quick Guide.
For journal articles, only use the formatting for the issue info “11, no. 1 (Spring): 95-109” if you are including the season. Otherwise, it should appear as “11 (1): 95–109”.

title: Style Guide
text:
Numerals
Spell out:

One through nine when not used with units of measurement or used in comparisons with numbers 10 or greater
Large numbers that can be expressed as two words (four hundred, two thousand)
Any number used to begin a sentence (unless it’s absolutely impossible to reword)
Numbers one or zero (zero-tolerance policy)
Common fractions (one-third)
Common expressions (twenty-first century)
Centuries (nineteenth century)

Use combination of words and numerals:

For large numbers (3 million people, 4.5 million dollars)
When numbers appears back-to-back (30 four-year-olds)

Use numerals:

For any number with a precise unit of measurement
To describe a sample size, specific number of participants
For measures of time, ages, dates, exact sums of money (8:00 am; $56.78)
For statistical or mathematical functions, proportions, ratios, percentages (use %)
Use numerals and spell out “percent” for non-technical contexts

title: Style Guide
text:
Tables
Titles and subtitles should sit outside of tables rather than inside a merged-across cell. Tables containing multiple sections titled or subtitled with merged-across cells should be broken into separate tables.

title: Style Guide
text:
General Style Guidelines

If a research article is based on a survey, we prefer to include the survey instrument in an appendix.
Avoid slang and colloquial language. The “take home message” is: don’t plan a library event on a Friday. Preferred style: In short: don’t plan a library event on a Friday.
Avoid needless words. Instead of a construction like “The question as to whether,” simply “Whether” would be preferred.


Rather than:
Therefore, this study reports on member perceptions of diversity through various aspects of board work such as…
The following is preferred:
This study reports on board member perceptions of diversity in the areas of…
Rather than:
in spite of the fact that
The following is preferred:
though or although
Rather than:
The job was unattractive in terms of salary
The following is preferred:
The salary made the job unattractive.


Use the appropriate prepositions for idiomatic phrases. When more than one phrase appears in a sentence, use the right preposition for each phrase:

Example:
His speech was marked by disagreement with and scorn for his opponent’s policies.

Avoid use of quotation marks to hedge or downplay meaning.


Correct: The teacher rewarded the class with tokens.
Incorrect: The teacher “rewarded” the class with tokens.


Avoid hedging words like apparently, comparatively, fairly, partially, relatively, unless absolutely necessary!
Avoid the abstract, vacuous language of metaconcepts (concepts that are containers for concepts).
Avoid nominalization (when a verb becomes an abstract noun) as much as possible. These are also known as “zombie nouns” because they lack a human agent. Look out for the long words that end in -ment, -ation, -ance and see if they can turn back into verbs instead.

E.g. We implemented a postponement of the event due to the weather.
Preferred style: We postponed the event due to the weather.

All acronyms must be spelled out in full the first time they are used in an article along with the acronym in parentheses. There are some exceptions—acronyms that all readers would be expected to know, and so would not need to be spelled out. (HTML, URL, MARC)
Spell out lesser known or unique acronyms (Rules for Archival Description, Metadata Object Description Schema, Ontario LIbrary Association. Unusual acronyms may be spelled in full throughout the article to take the burden off the reader to remember what they stand for.

Spacing between list items
By default there will be a empty line between bullet points. That’s usually undesirable unless the bullets contain long multi-line text and spacing them out improves readability. So you will often use \tightlist to reduce the space between the items. Like this:
\begin{itemize}

  \item this is the third bullet point

title: Tables
Tables
text:
Table Position
LaTeX will not always put your table exactly where you placed it in the text due to its internal layout rules. If the default position is not ideal, you can attempt giving LaTeX some instructions to better position the table.
If you’re happy with the table placement, you don’t have to do anything.

Specifiers







Specifier
Meaning




h
Place the table here, roughly at the current location


t
Place the table at the top of the page


b
Place the table at the bottom of the page


p
Place the table on a separate page for floats only


!
Override LaTeX’s internal float placement rules


H
Place the table exactly here (requires float package)





Example
\begin{table*}
  \begin{longtable}
  \end{longtable}
\end{table*}


Tips and tricks

You can combine them (e.g.,[htbp!] )to give LaTeX flexibility while nudging it toward your preferred location.
It is recommended not to use [h] alone, as it can sometimes be ignored. Prefer [ht] or [htbp].







Do not fight LaTeX



Often, you might find that latex is not at all cooperating with you when it comes to positioning tables. My advice is to not die on that hill. Your table is showing up somewhere in the document. It looks good, but it’s not where you want it, so you spend a few minutes trying different strategies to move it to a better spot. No luck? Just move on.

text:
Columns

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{1.5in} 
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.5in}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{2.5in} 
}

Alignment

left: \raggedright\arraybackslash
center: \centeringt\arraybackslash
right: \raggedleftt\arraybackslash



Column width
the {\textwidth} part of the code above ensures sets your table to cover the whole horizontal space it has available.
The dimentions indicated in the format p{1.5in} is the part that actually sets the width of the column. You should make sure that the column width is optimal for the content, and that the total of all the column width is equal to the witdth of the horizontal space availabe.
For single column table, the total available space is 8.65cm or 3.41in. For a two-column table, the total available space is about 16.51cm or 6.5in. As you can see in the latex code above, the total for the three column is actually 6.5 inches because the table is spanning two columns (as indicated by the use of tabularx.

title: Tables
Tables
text:
Rows

Each cell is separated by an ampersand (&).
Each row ends with two backslashes (linebreak): \\

Here is an example.
first cell content & second cell content & third cell content \\

title: Tables
text:
Borders

\toprule for the boder at the top of the table.
\midrule for the border below the header row.
\bottomrule for the border at the end of the table.
\cline{} for a line that doesn’t go across the entire table but just for a specific set of columns. For example, \cline{2-3} will draw a line only for columns 2 and 3.

Here is an example. Note that the \textbf{} is used to make the column header bold, which is the standard practice for CJILS manuscript.
\toprule
\textbf{First name} & \textbf{Last name} & \textbf{Date of birth} \\
\midrule
John & Smith & July 14, 1975 \\
Mary & Robinson & March 6, 1979 \\
\bottomrule

title: Tables
text:
Merging rows and columns

Merging columns
If you want for a cell to span two columns, you can do this with \multicolumn{}{}{}. The first curly bracket is for the numbers of columns to span, the second is for alignment (l, c, or r), and the third is for the content. Here is an example where I merge the last two columns for the first row. The table has three columns, so every row should have two &. However, we can see that the first row as only one & and a cell spanning 2 columns.
  \begin{tabular}{
    >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.25cm}
    >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{1cm}
    >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{1cm}
  }
  \toprule
   & \multicolumn{2}{r}{Publication} \\
  Country & N & Pct. \\
  \midrule
  Canada & 20 & 80\% \\
  United States & 5 & 20\% \\
  \bottomrule


Merging rows
Merging rows kind of works the same way with \multirow{number of rows}{*}{content}.I’m not too sure what the star does, but it’s normally there.
  \toprule
  \multirow{2}{*}{Country} & \multicolumn{2}{r}{Publication} \\
  & N & Pct. \\
  \midrule
  Canada & 20 & 80\% \\
  United States & 5 & 20\% \\
  \bottomrule

text:
Notes
Adding footnotes to a table is done manually, by adding the a superscript in the cell that will refer to the note, and then adding a row that spans all columns at the end of the table. Note that the \\[-1.75ex] is there to add a small space between the last column and the footnote.
\toprule
\textbf{First name} & \textbf{Last name} & \textbf{Date of birth}
\bottomrule\textit{\textsuperscript{*}} \\
\midrule
John & Smith & July 14, 1975 \\
Mary & Robinson & March 6, 1979 \\
\bottomrule
\\[-1.75ex]
\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textsuperscript{*}This is a table not related to the date of birth column.} \\

title: Tables
Tables
text:
Tips and tricks

Copy pasting from Word
You don’t need to design your table from scratch, when in visual mode in Overleaf, you can copy and paste the table from word and you will just have to edit the automatically generated code rather than starting from scratch. This can save a lot of time.


Copilot
Copilot (or other AI tools I would imagine) can help you fix your table…. it’s not working. Copy your entire code from \begin{table} to \end{table} in a prompt that looks like this:

This does not work:
[paste your code here.]

Of course, you can be more specific about the issue.

title: References
text:
Tip and tricks
references start with \begin{CSLReferences}{1}{} and end with \end{CSLReferences}.
Each reference is a \bititem{}. You can write a label for each reference (e.g. \bibitem{abedin2018}) but it`s not necessary. The references should be formatted according to the APA 7 format, manually (but see the tips and tricks below for a time saver).
You can give the list of references to Copilot and ask it to format it for you and even get the DOIs.
